_note: “Did you know?” box on the printable sheet of a word set (src/pages/wortschatz/drucken/[set].astro): three short facts about the topic, in the English of the level. Machine draft 2026-10-30, not yet reviewed by a teacher.
a1-01: In a UK address the number comes before the street: 5 High Street.
‘Ms’ can be used for any woman. ‘Mr’, ‘Mrs’ and ‘Ms’ go before the family name.
‘How are you?’ is often just a way to say hello. People usually answer ‘Fine, thanks’.
a1-02: ‘Grandma’ and ‘Grandpa’ are friendly words. ‘Grandmother’ and ‘Grandfather’ are more formal.
‘Cousin’ is for a man or a woman.
a1-03: ‘Fine’ and ‘OK’ are common answers to ‘How are you?’
‘Bored’ is how you feel. ‘Boring’ is the thing. A boring film makes me bored.
‘Happy’ is a feeling. ‘Unhappy’ is the opposite.
a1-04: In the UK the ground floor is at street level. The next floor is the first floor.
A ‘flat’ is a home in a building with other homes. Americans say ‘apartment’.
A British house can have a toilet in a separate small room, not in the bathroom.
a1-05: ‘Sofa’, ‘settee’ and ‘couch’ mean nearly the same thing.
A UK plug has three pins.
a1-06: In the UK, ‘chips’ are fried potatoes. Americans call them ‘fries’.
Many people in the UK drink tea with milk.
In some parts of the UK, ‘tea’ also means the evening meal.
a1-07: UK money is the pound (£). There are 100 pence in a pound.
In England, shops must charge for plastic bags.
British people say ‘shop’. Americans often say ‘store’.
a1-08: In British English, ‘trousers’. In American English, ‘pants’.
British English writes ‘colour’. American English writes ‘color’.
a1-09: We say ‘I have a headache’. We say ‘My head hurts’, too.
One foot, two feet. One tooth, two teeth.
In British English, ‘ill’ means not well. ‘Sick’ often means you vomit.
a1-10: A family doctor in the UK is a ‘GP’. It means General Practitioner.
You usually make an appointment to see the GP.
The emergency number in the UK is 999.
a1-11: We say ‘have breakfast’ and ‘have a shower’.
We say ‘in the morning’, ‘in the afternoon’ and ‘in the evening’. But we say ‘at night’.
‘Nine to five’ means normal office hours.
a1-12: ‘Work’ is not countable. We do not say ‘a work’. We say ‘a job’.
With jobs we use ‘a’ or ‘an’: I’m a teacher. She’s an engineer.
A ‘boss’ is the person above you at work.
a1-13: Children in England start school at four or five.
In British English, ‘maths’. In American English, ‘math’.
A child at school is often a ‘pupil’. A person at university is a ‘student’.
a1-14: ‘Football’ in the UK is ‘soccer’ in the USA.
We say ‘play tennis’, ‘go swimming’ and ‘do yoga’.
‘Hobby’ is a thing you like to do in your free time.
a1-15: The ‘High Street’ is the main shopping street in many UK towns.
British English says ‘town centre’. American English says ‘downtown’.
a1-16: In the UK, cars drive on the left.
In London, the train under the ground is the ‘Underground’ or the ‘Tube’.
British English says ‘pavement’. American English says ‘sidewalk’.
a1-17: ‘Luggage’ has no plural. We say ‘two bags’, not ‘two luggages’.
We say ‘on holiday’: I’m on holiday this week.
a1-18: In the UK, 30/10/2026 is 30 October. The day comes first.
Zero can be ‘zero’, ‘nought’ or ‘oh’. In phone numbers people often say ‘oh’.
a1-19: We use ‘it’ for weather: It’s raining. It’s cold.
People in the UK often talk about the weather to start a conversation.
Americans often say ‘fall’. British English says ‘autumn’.
a1-20: ‘Sheep’ is singular and plural: one sheep, two sheep.
One mouse, two mice. One goose, two geese.
A baby cat is a ‘kitten’. A baby dog is a ‘puppy’.
a1-21: We use ‘have’ in many phrases: have lunch, have a shower, have a good time.
We ‘do’ homework, but we ‘make’ a cup of tea.
a1-22: We ‘watch’ TV, but we ‘look at’ a picture.
We ‘say’ hello, but we ‘tell’ someone a story.
a1-23: Add ‘un-’ to make some opposites: happy – unhappy, kind – unkind.
‘Big’ and ‘large’ are nearly the same. ‘Large’ is a bit more formal.
The opposite of ‘old’ can be ‘young’ or ‘new’.
a1-24: We say ‘at 6 o’clock’, ‘on Monday’ and ‘in July’.
We say ‘at home’ and ‘go home’. We do not say ‘to home’.
a1-25: ‘The’ is the most common word in English.
People in the UK say ‘please’ and ‘thank you’ a lot.
a1-26: ‘Surname’, ‘family name’ and ‘last name’ mean the same.
A UK postcode has letters and numbers, for example SW1A 1AA.
a2-01: In UK adverts, ‘pcm’ means ‘per calendar month’. It is the rent for one month.
A ‘deposit’ is money you pay at the start. You get it back if you leave the home in good condition.
‘Furnished’ means the flat has furniture. ‘Unfurnished’ means it has none.
a2-02: ‘Neighbour’ has ‘ou’ in British English. In American English it is ‘neighbor’.
The ‘next-door neighbour’ lives in the house or flat beside yours.
You borrow sugar from a neighbour. A neighbour lends it to you.
a2-03: In British English, ‘do the washing-up’ means wash the dishes.
‘Hoover’ is a brand name. In British English, ‘to hoover’ means to clean with a vacuum cleaner.
We ‘do’ the housework, but we ‘make’ the bed.
a2-04: British English says ‘aubergine’ and ‘courgette’. American English says ‘eggplant’ and ‘zucchini’.
You ‘bake’ a cake in the oven, ‘fry’ an egg in a pan and ‘boil’ pasta in water.
In recipes, ‘tsp’ is a teaspoon and ‘tbsp’ is a tablespoon.
a2-05: In the UK you ask for ‘the bill’. In the USA people say ‘the check’.
A menu often has a ‘starter’, a ‘main course’ and a ‘dessert’.
A restaurant sometimes adds a service charge to the bill. Check the bill before you add a tip.
a2-06: We say ‘I have a cold’ with ‘a’. We say ‘I have flu’ or ‘the flu’.
The NHS is the UK’s public health service. Most care is free for people who live there.
a2-07: In the UK you can say ‘chemist’ or ‘pharmacy’. In the USA people say ‘drugstore’.
‘Paracetamol’ is the British name. Americans say ‘acetaminophen’.
Some medicines need a prescription from a doctor.
a2-08: We say ‘brush your teeth’ and ‘wash your hands’, with ‘your’, not ‘the’.
A ‘barber’ usually cuts men’s hair. A ‘hairdresser’ cuts hair for everyone.
In British English we ‘have a shower’. In American English people often ‘take a shower’.
a2-09: In the UK it is a ‘CV’ (curriculum vitae). In the USA it is a ‘résumé’.
A ‘covering letter’ goes with your CV and says why you want the job.
A ‘referee’ is a person who can say good things about you. Their opinion is a ‘reference’.
a2-10: ‘Colleague’ means a person you work with.
‘Staff’ means all the people who work in a company. We do not say ‘a staff’ for one person.
a2-11: You can ‘take a course’ or ‘do a course’. Both are fine in British English.
An ‘apprenticeship’ is a job with training. Apprentices earn money while they learn.
A ‘certificate’ is a paper that shows you passed a course.
a2-12: A UK bank account has a six-digit sort code and an eight-digit account number.
British English says ‘current account’. American English says ‘checking account’.
‘Contactless’ means you pay by touching your card or phone on the machine.
a2-13: British English says ‘post’. American English says ‘mail’.
Many British post boxes are red.
In the UK you can buy first-class or second-class stamps. First class is faster.
a2-14: In the UK, adults who work have a National Insurance number (NI number).
British English often says ‘fill in a form’. Americans say ‘fill out a form’.
a2-15: A letter or email starting ‘Dear Mr Smith’ ends with ‘Yours sincerely’. After ‘Dear Sir or Madam’ it ends with ‘Yours faithfully’.
British English says ‘mobile phone’. American English says ‘cell phone’.
‘CC’ in an email means ‘carbon copy’. The other person gets a copy.
a2-16: ‘Log in’ is a verb with two words. ‘Login’ is a noun.
Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, invented the World Wide Web around 1989.
a2-17: A ‘refund’ gives you your money back. An ‘exchange’ gives you another item.
A polite way to complain: ‘I’m afraid there is a problem with this.’
a2-18: In the UK a ‘single’ ticket is one way. A ‘return’ ticket is there and back.
In London you can pay with an Oyster card or a contactless bank card.
On the London Underground you hear ‘Mind the gap’ at the platform.
a2-19: In the UK the steering wheel is on the right and you drive on the left.
British English says ‘petrol’. American English says ‘gas’.
British English says ‘boot’ and ‘bonnet’. American English says ‘trunk’ and ‘hood’.
a2-20: ‘Book a room’ means the same as ‘reserve a room’.
At a hotel there is often a time for ‘check-in’ and a time for ‘check-out’.
a2-21: In the UK, 26 December is called Boxing Day. It is a public holiday.
Bonfire Night is on 5 November. People watch fireworks.
A ‘bank holiday’ is a public holiday in the UK.
a2-22: The modern rules of football were first written in England in 1863.
Wimbledon is a famous tennis tournament in London.
We say ‘play tennis’, ‘go for a run’ and ‘do yoga’.
a2-23: British English says ‘film’ and ‘cinema’. American English says ‘movie’ and ‘movie theater’.
William Shakespeare wrote more than 30 plays.
We ‘read’ a book, ‘watch’ a film and ‘listen to’ music.
a2-24: ‘Sensible’ means practical and careful. It does not mean ‘sensitive’.
‘Easy-going’ describes a person who does not worry a lot.
a2-25: We say ‘I agree’, not ‘I am agree’.
‘Excited’ is the feeling. ‘Exciting’ is the thing.
In British English, ‘not bad’ often means ‘quite good’.
a2-26: Recycling rules are different in different parts of the UK.
British English says ‘rubbish’. American English says ‘garbage’ or ‘trash’.
‘Litter’ is rubbish that people leave in the street or in a park.
a2-27: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, for example ‘give up’. The meaning is often new.
Some phrasal verbs can split: ‘turn off the light’ or ‘turn the light off’. With ‘it’ we say ‘turn it off’.
‘Get’ makes many phrasal verbs: get up, get on, get off, get back.
a2-28: ‘Could you …?’ is more polite than ‘Can you …?’
We use ‘Would you like …?’ for offers and ‘How about …?’ for suggestions.
In the UK, ‘cheers’ can mean ‘thank you’.
b1-01: The ‘notice period’ is the time between telling your employer you are leaving and your last day.
In British English, ‘redundancy’ means you lose your job because the employer no longer needs the role. It is not about your work.
‘Dismissed’ is the formal word. People often say ‘sacked’ or ‘fired’.
b1-02: The NHS (National Health Service) started in 1948.
In the UK, you usually see a GP first. For a specialist you normally need a referral from the GP.
‘A&E’ stands for ‘Accident and Emergency’. Americans say ‘ER’.
b1-03: A ‘letting agent’ finds tenants for a landlord. A ‘To Let’ sign means a property is for rent.
In England the most common rental contract is an ‘assured shorthold tenancy’.
‘Tenant’ is the person who rents. ‘Landlord’ or ‘landlady’ is the person who owns the home.
b1-04: A passport shows who you are. A visa is permission to enter or stay in a country.
‘Leave to remain’ is a UK phrase for permission to stay in the country.
A document is ‘valid’ if it has not expired.
b1-05: In the UK, ‘further education’ is education after school that is not a university degree. ‘Higher education’ is university.
A ‘qualification’ is any certificate you earn. A ‘degree’ is a university qualification.
‘CPD’ means ‘continuing professional development’: learning during your working life.
b1-06: The UK has a law to reach ‘net zero’ greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
‘Renewable’ energy comes from sources that do not run out, like wind, sun and water.
Your ‘carbon footprint’ is the amount of carbon dioxide linked to your way of life.
b1-07: ‘Quid’ is an informal word for pounds. A ‘fiver’ is £5 and a ‘tenner’ is £10.
VAT means ‘value added tax’. The standard rate in the UK is 20 per cent.
You pay with a ‘debit card’ from your own money. A ‘credit card’ lends you money.
b1-08: At a UK roundabout you go clockwise and give way to traffic from the right.
British English says ‘motorway’. American English says ‘highway’ or ‘freeway’.
Speed limits in the UK are in miles per hour.
b1-09: In the UK you need a TV licence to watch live TV or BBC iPlayer.
A ‘tabloid’ is a smaller newspaper with short, simple stories. A ‘broadsheet’ has longer, more serious articles.
‘Breaking news’ is news that has just happened.
b1-10: ‘Small talk’ is polite, light conversation, for example about the weather.
British English often uses softeners: ‘I’m afraid …’, ‘sort of’, ‘a bit’.
‘Let’s agree to disagree’ means both people keep their own opinion.
b1-11: Citizens Advice is a UK charity that gives free advice on money, housing and rights.
A ‘charity shop’ sells second-hand things to raise money for a good cause.
The ‘council’ is the local government of a town or area.
b1-12: ‘The small print’ is the detailed text in a contract. People say ‘Always read the small print’.
A ‘legally binding’ agreement is one you must follow by law.
b1-13: The word ‘spam’ for junk email comes from a Monty Python sketch about tinned meat.
‘Online’ means connected to the internet. ‘Offline’ is the opposite.
b1-14: A ‘pub quiz’ is a popular evening in many UK pubs. Teams answer general-knowledge questions.
You ‘join’ a club and then you are a ‘member’.
‘parkrun’ is a free weekly 5 km run in parks. It started in London in 2004.
b1-15: ‘Travel’ is a general word. A ‘journey’ is one trip from one place to another.
British English writes ‘cancelled’ with two ‘l’s. American English often writes ‘canceled’.
A ‘package holiday’ includes travel and hotel in one price.
b1-16: The word ‘vegan’ was created in England in 1944 by Donald Watson.
‘Use by’ is about safety. ‘Best before’ is about quality.
A ‘ready meal’ is food you only have to heat up.
b1-17: You ‘emigrate’ from a country and ‘immigrate’ to a country.
‘Culture shock’ is the strange feeling in a new country where everything is different.
When you move to the UK, you can register with a local GP.
b1-18: The UK Parliament has two houses: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
An ‘MP’ is a Member of Parliament.
The Prime Minister’s official home is 10 Downing Street in London.
b1-19: A ‘zero-hours contract’ gives you no fixed number of working hours.
In the UK there is a National Minimum Wage and a National Living Wage.
b1-20: Pancake Day is Shrove Tuesday, the day before the Christian period of Lent.
On Remembrance Sunday in November, many people in the UK wear a red poppy.
Burns Night on 25 January remembers the Scottish poet Robert Burns.
b1-21: We say ‘I’m looking forward to meeting you’, with the ‘-ing’ form.
‘Mixed feelings’ means you feel good and bad about the same thing.
‘Make up your mind’ means decide. ‘Change your mind’ means decide something different.
b1-22: English has many idioms with body parts: ‘keep an eye on’, ‘lend a hand’.
‘Stroll’ means to walk slowly and calmly.
If you ‘sprain’ your ankle, you hurt it by twisting it.
b1-23: ‘Bring up’ is common in British English. ‘Raise’ is common in American English.
In the UK, parents can take maternity or paternity leave.
A ‘single parent’ looks after a child alone.
b1-24: In the UK, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says goods must be of satisfactory quality and as described.
A ‘guarantee’ is a promise from the seller to repair or replace a faulty product.
After Christmas, many UK shops have the Boxing Day sales.
b1-25: The ‘outskirts’ are the parts of a town far from the centre.
‘Cul-de-sac’ comes from French and means ‘bottom of the bag’. It is a street with only one way in.
A ‘corner shop’ is a small local shop.
b1-26: Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the UK, at 1,345 metres.
In Scotland, a ‘loch’ is a lake.
b1-27: ‘Weather’ is what it is like today. ‘Climate’ is the usual weather over many years.
b1-28: After the Norman conquest in 1066, thousands of French words came into English.
English spelling does not always match the sound: ‘though’, ‘through’ and ‘tough’ all end in ‘-ough’.
You ‘learn’ a language yourself. A teacher ‘teaches’ you.
b1-29: ‘Smart casual’ is a dress code between formal and relaxed.
Clothes ‘fit’ you if the size is right. A colour ‘suits’ you if you look good in it.
‘Try on’ clothes in the shop before you buy them.
b1-30: ‘On time’ means at the right time. ‘In time’ means early enough.
A ‘fortnight’ is two weeks. It is a British word.
Timetables often use the 24-hour clock: 18:30 is half past six in the evening.
b1-31: The word ‘scientist’ was first used by William Whewell in 1833.
b1-32: ‘Annual leave’ is paid holiday. By law, most workers in the UK get at least 5.6 weeks a year.
A ‘promotion’ is a move to a better job in the same company.
‘Work-life balance’ means the balance between work and private life.
b1-33: A ‘ward’ is a room or part of a hospital for patients.
An ‘inpatient’ stays in hospital. An ‘outpatient’ comes for treatment and goes home the same day.
b1-34: ‘Council tax’ is a local tax that households in the UK pay.
Utility bills are for gas, electricity and water.
A ‘standing charge’ is a fixed daily amount on your energy bill.
b1-35: In British English, ‘benefits’ are payments from the state. Universal Credit is one of them.
You ‘claim’ a benefit. You are ‘entitled to’ it if you meet the rules.
Many applications in the UK are made online.
b1-36: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, pupils usually take GCSEs at 16 and A levels at 18.
Scotland has a different system, with National 5s and Highers.
A ‘public school’ in England is a private school you pay for.
b1-37: ‘Income’ is the money you receive. ‘Outgoings’ is the money you spend regularly.
An ISA is a savings account in the UK where you do not pay tax on the interest.
‘Save up for’ means keep money for a goal. ‘Pay off’ a debt means pay all of it.
b1-38: The Highway Code is the official book of road rules in the UK.
A ‘zebra crossing’ has black and white stripes, like a zebra.
In the UK, a car usually needs an MOT test every year once it is three years old.
b1-39: ‘Misinformation’ is false information, even if someone shares it by mistake. ‘Disinformation’ is spread on purpose.
A ‘reliable’ source is one you can trust.
To ‘fact-check’ means to check if something is true.
b1-40: We ‘agree with’ a person, ‘agree to’ a plan and ‘agree on’ a decision.
A ‘compromise’ is an agreement where both sides give up something.
‘Meet someone halfway’ means accept a compromise.
b1-41: ‘Volunteer’ can be a noun or a verb: She volunteers at a food bank.
A ‘charity’ is an organisation that raises money for good causes.
‘Voluntary’ means done by choice, often without pay.
b1-42: In the UK, 999 is for emergencies and 101 is for police matters that are not urgent.
‘Bobby’ is an old nickname for a British police officer. It comes from Sir Robert Peel, who set up the Metropolitan Police in 1829.
A ‘burglary’ is breaking into a building to steal. A ‘robbery’ uses force or threats against a person.
b1-43: British English says ‘spanner’. American English says ‘wrench’.
‘DIY’ means ‘do it yourself’: repairing or building things at home.
‘Measure twice, cut once’ is a good rule in the workshop.
b1-44: In England and Wales there are thousands of miles of public footpaths.
British English often says ‘walking’ or ‘rambling’ for what Americans call ‘hiking’.
We say ‘go hiking’, ‘go camping’ and ‘go climbing’.
b1-45: British English says ‘junction’. American English says ‘intersection’.
‘Sat nav’ is the British short form of ‘satellite navigation’.
‘Take the second turning on the left’ is a typical way to give directions.
b1-46: A ‘takeaway’ is food you buy to eat at home. Americans say ‘takeout’.
A ‘full English’ is a big breakfast with eggs, bacon, sausage and more.
In many UK restaurants a tip of about 10 to 12.5 per cent is usual, sometimes added to the bill as a service charge.
b2-01: To ‘delegate’ means to give a task to someone else.
‘CEO’ means ‘chief executive officer’. In the UK people also say ‘managing director’.
Your ‘line manager’ is the person you report to directly.
b2-02: British English writes ‘globalisation’ with an ‘s’. American English writes ‘globalization’.
The FTSE 100 is an index of the 100 biggest companies on the London Stock Exchange.
A ‘tariff’ is a tax on goods that come into a country.
b2-03: ‘Liable’ means legally responsible. Do not confuse it with ‘likely’.
English contracts use Latin and French phrases such as ‘pro rata’ and ‘force majeure’.
A ‘breach of contract’ happens when one side does not keep the agreement.
b2-04: The UK has no single written constitution document.
The Speaker is the MP who chairs debates in the House of Commons.
‘Hansard’ is the official record of what is said in Parliament.
b2-05: British English writes ‘ageing’. American English writes ‘aging’.
The UK holds a census every ten years. The last one was in 2021.
‘Baby boomers’ were born in the years after the Second World War.
b2-06: ‘Net zero’ means the greenhouse gases we add equal the ones we remove.
The 2021 UN climate conference, COP26, was held in Glasgow.
‘Fossil fuels’ such as coal, oil and gas formed from ancient plants and animals.
b2-07: ‘Phishing’ sounds like ‘fishing’. Criminals use fake messages to catch your data.
In the UK, data protection is covered by UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.
With ‘end-to-end encryption’ only the sender and receiver can read a message.
b2-08: ‘Data’ is the plural of ‘datum’, but it is now often used as an uncountable noun.
‘Correlation does not imply causation’: two things happening together does not mean one causes the other.
A larger ‘sample size’ usually gives more reliable results.
b2-09: Fleet Street in London was for a long time the home of British newspapers. The name is still used for the press.
An ‘op-ed’ is an opinion piece, often by a guest writer.
An ‘editorial’ shows the opinion of the newspaper itself.
b2-10: Teaching at the University of Oxford goes back to at least 1096.
In England, a bachelor’s degree usually takes three years. A first-year student is a ‘fresher’.
A ‘viva’ is an oral exam, for example on your thesis.
b2-11: ‘Prevention is better than cure’ is a well-known saying about health.
An ‘epidemic’ spreads in one area. A ‘pandemic’ spreads across many countries.
‘Screening’ means testing people who have no symptoms.
b2-12: ‘CBT’ means ‘cognitive behavioural therapy’. Americans spell it ‘behavioral’.
To ‘cope with’ stress means to manage it.
‘Burnout’ is a state of complete exhaustion from long-term stress.
b2-13: An ‘asylum seeker’ has applied for protection and is waiting for a decision. A ‘refugee’ has been recognised as needing protection.
The 1951 Refugee Convention defines who is a refugee.
‘Belongings’ are your things. ‘Belonging’ is the feeling of being part of a group.
b2-14: Stonehenge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The National Trust is a British charity, founded in 1895, that looks after historic places and nature.
A ‘listed building’ in the UK is legally protected because of its history or architecture.
b2-15: ‘Register’ means how formal or informal your language is.
Phrasal verbs are often more informal than single verbs: ‘get’ is more informal than ‘obtain’.
Contractions like ‘don’t’ are normal in informal writing but are usually avoided in formal writing.
b2-16: The ‘green belt’ is protected land around some English cities. It stops towns from growing into the countryside.
A ‘terraced’ house is in a row. A ‘semi-detached’ house is joined to one other house.
‘Affordable housing’ is housing that people on lower incomes can pay for.
b2-17: A ‘Site of Special Scientific Interest’ (SSSI) is a protected area in Great Britain.
‘Rewilding’ means returning land to its natural state.
An ‘endangered species’ is a type of animal or plant that may die out.
b2-18: In the UK, ‘shares’ are the usual word. Americans often say ‘stocks’.
‘Blue chip’ companies are large and reliable. The name comes from the most valuable chips in poker.
To ‘diversify’ means to spread your money across different investments.
b2-19: The world’s first underground railway opened in London in 1863.
London has had a congestion charge for drivers in the centre since 2003.
‘Commute’ can be a verb or a noun: a long commute.
b2-20: In British English we ‘appeal against’ a decision.
‘Ombudsman’ is a Swedish word. An ombudsman investigates complaints about public bodies.
‘Red tape’ means too many official rules. It comes from the red ribbon once used to tie official papers.
b2-21: The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is the UK body for workplace safety.
A ‘risk assessment’ is a check of what could go wrong and how to prevent it.
In the UK, the average working week is limited to 48 hours unless you choose to opt out.
b2-22: In the UK, the Food Standards Agency gives restaurants a hygiene rating from 0 to 5.
UK law says food businesses must tell you about 14 main allergens.
‘From farm to fork’ describes the whole path of food from the farm to the plate.
b2-23: Rugby is named after Rugby School in England.
A ‘fixture’ is a match that is planned for a certain date.
An ‘amateur’ plays for fun. A ‘professional’ is paid.
b2-24: British English says ‘carer’. American English says ‘caregiver’.
The ‘sandwich generation’ looks after both their children and their ageing parents.
Carer’s Allowance is a UK benefit for some people who look after someone.
b2-25: A ‘comprehensive’ school in England takes pupils of all abilities.
A ‘grammar school’ in England is selective. Pupils take an exam at age 11.
‘Widening participation’ means helping more people from all backgrounds to go to university.
b2-26: A ‘win-win’ situation is good for both sides.
‘Persuade’ someone to do something. ‘Convince’ someone that something is true.
‘Common ground’ is what both sides already agree on.
b2-27: ‘Peer pressure’ is the pressure to do what people of your age or group do.
‘Intrinsic’ motivation comes from inside you. ‘Extrinsic’ motivation comes from rewards.
‘Herd mentality’ is when people copy what the crowd does.
b2-28: ‘Slogan’ comes from a Gaelic word for a battle cry.
A ‘USP’ is a ‘unique selling point’: what makes a product different.
In the UK, the Advertising Standards Authority checks that adverts are honest.
b2-29: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century.
‘Manufacture’ comes from Latin words meaning ‘made by hand’.
The National Grid is the network that carries electricity across Great Britain.
b2-30: A ‘sole trader’ is a self-employed person who runs a business alone.
Companies House is the UK register of companies.
b2-31: ‘Informed consent’ means a patient agrees to treatment after getting clear information.
A patient can ask for a ‘second opinion’ from another doctor.
Patient ‘confidentiality’ means a doctor must keep your information private.
b2-32: ‘Mitigation’ reduces the causes of climate change. ‘Adaptation’ deals with its effects.
British English writes ‘defences’. American English writes ‘defenses’.
To ‘evacuate’ means to leave a dangerous place.
b2-33: Magna Carta, from 1215, is an early English document that limited the power of the king.
A ‘whistleblower’ is a person who reports wrongdoing inside an organisation.
‘Habeas corpus’ is a Latin legal term. It protects people from unlawful detention.
b2-34: ‘Safeguarding’ is a UK term for protecting children and vulnerable adults from harm.
A ‘food bank’ gives free food to people who cannot afford it.
In the UK, the ‘local authority’ is the council that provides local services.
b2-35: The Skilled Worker visa is a UK visa for people with a job offer from an approved employer.
‘Brain drain’ is when many skilled people leave a country.
A ‘sponsor’ is an employer that supports a visa application.
b2-36: The UK’s foreign ministry is the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.
The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
A ‘summit’ is a meeting between leaders of countries.
b2-37: In ‘peer review’, other experts check a study before it is published.
‘Plagiarism’ comes from a Latin word for ‘kidnapper’.
An ‘ethics committee’ must approve many studies that involve people.
b2-38: An ‘aquifer’ is underground rock that holds water. The word comes from Latin ‘aqua’ (water).
In the UK, a ‘hosepipe ban’ stops people using hoses in dry weather.
b2-39: The BAFTA awards are British film and television prizes.
b2-40: A ‘toddler’ is a child who has just learned to walk.
The ‘generation gap’ is the difference in views between older and younger people.
b2-41: Savile Row in London is famous for ‘bespoke’ suits, made specially for one customer.
‘Fast fashion’ is cheap clothing made quickly to follow trends.
In the Industrial Revolution, textile mills, especially for cotton, were among the first big factories.
b2-42: The Met Office is the UK’s national weather service.
The Shipping Forecast on BBC Radio 4 is a weather report for the seas around Britain.
A ‘heatwave’ is a period of unusually hot weather.
b2-43: A ‘biography’ is written by someone else. An ‘autobiography’ is written by the person themselves.
A ‘memoir’ is a book about a part of your own life.
‘Heritage’ can mean the culture and traditions you inherit from your family.
b2-44: ‘Moody’ describes a person whose mood changes often.
‘Mood’ and ‘mode’ look similar but have different meanings.
In English, ‘feeling blue’ means feeling sad.
b2-45: In the UK, you usually have a 14-day cooling-off period to cancel most online purchases.
Trading Standards is a UK service that enforces consumer law.
‘Retail’ means selling to the public. ‘Wholesale’ means selling in large amounts to businesses.
b2-46: ‘Ergonomic’ comes from Greek words meaning ‘work’ and ‘rules’.
You ‘strain’ a muscle but ‘sprain’ a ligament.
b2-47: ‘Deadline’ was first a line around a prison camp in the American Civil War.
‘Ahead of schedule’ means early. ‘Behind schedule’ means late.
b2-48: A ‘contingency plan’ is a plan B for when things go wrong.
If you are ‘stranded’, you cannot leave a place, for example because of cancelled trains.
‘Travel insurance’ can pay for costs if a trip is cancelled or you get ill.
b2-49: In England, a home can be ‘freehold’ or ‘leasehold’. Leasehold means you own it for a fixed number of years.
‘Mortgage’ comes from Old French and means ‘dead pledge’.
‘Conveyancing’ is the legal process of buying or selling a property.
b2-50: Georgian houses in England date from the 18th and early 19th century.
In London, a ‘blue plaque’ on a building shows that a famous person lived or worked there.
‘Victorian’ describes the time of Queen Victoria, who ruled from 1837 to 1901.
b2-51: A ‘councillor’ is an elected member of a local council.
UK general elections use the ‘first past the post’ system: the candidate with the most votes wins the seat.
A ‘polling station’ is the place where people vote.
b2-52: The Royal Society, a famous science organisation in London, was founded in 1660.
In science, a ‘theory’ is a well-tested explanation. In everyday English it can mean just a guess.
‘Peer-reviewed’ research has been checked by other experts.
b2-53: A ‘recession’ is often defined as two quarters in a row of falling GDP.
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate for the UK.
b2-54: Magistrates’ courts deal with less serious crimes in England and Wales.
In England and Wales, a jury has twelve members.
A ‘barrister’ speaks in court. A ‘solicitor’ usually gives legal advice and prepares cases.
b2-55: ‘Fly-tipping’ is the illegal dumping of waste in the UK.
A ‘circular economy’ reuses and recycles materials instead of throwing them away.
‘Landfill’ is a place where rubbish is buried.
b2-56: In British English you ‘sit’ an exam. It means take it.
British English says ‘mark’. American English says ‘grade’.
‘Formative’ assessment helps you learn. ‘Summative’ assessment gives a final result.
b2-57: ‘Robot’ comes from a Czech word for forced labour. It was made popular by a 1920 play by Karel Čapek.
Alan Turing, a British mathematician, suggested the ‘Turing test’ in 1950.
‘Algorithm’ comes from the name of the mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
b2-58: The word ‘viral’ comes from ‘virus’: something that spreads quickly.
A ‘troll’ is a person who posts offensive messages online to cause a reaction.
An ‘influencer’ is a person with many followers who can affect what others buy.
b2-59: ‘Agenda’ comes from Latin as a plural, but in English it is singular: ‘The agenda is long.’
‘Minutes’ are the written record of a meeting.
‘AOB’ on a UK agenda means ‘any other business’.
b2-60: English has more non-native speakers than native speakers.
Welsh is an official language in Wales, together with English.
‘False friends’ are words that look similar in two languages but have different meanings.
